summary: This memo gives a brief overview of the Standing Documents series from the North American Directory Forum, which dealt with running X.500 directory services in North America. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 1758.

eli5.summary: A group of people running online phone books wrote a set of rule documents. This paper is a short guide to what is in that set. A newer guide replaced it.

subtitle: A short guide to the document series that let competing providers run one public X.500 directory.

tldr.problem: Competing service providers wanted to offer one cooperative Public Directory Service in North America using the CCITT X.500 Recommendations, and they needed written agreements to do it.
tldr.mechanism: The North American Directory Forum (NADF) wrote a numbered series of Standing Documents (SD-0 to SD-12), and this memo briefly describes what each one covers and how to get copies.
tldr.outcome: This memo was obsoleted by RFC 1758, which replaces this overview of the series.

today: RFC 1417 is Informational and has been obsoleted by RFC 1758, so it is only a historical overview of the NADF series.

sections.title: Why the NADF Wrote Standing Documents
sections.content:
The North American Directory Forum (NADF) is a collection of service providers that plans to offer a Public Directory Service in North America using the CCITT X.500 Recommendations. The RFC says the NADF is unusual because it must achieve a cooperative service offered by competing providers.

This memo is an informational overview of the NADF Standing Document series. It obsoletes RFC 1295, RFC 1255 and RFC 1218, and says it does not specify an Internet standard.
sections.eli5: Imagine rival shops agreeing to share one town directory. They have to write down the rules first, and this memo lists those rules.

sections.title: The Documents in the Series
sections.content:
The series runs from SD-0 (this overview) to SD-12. SD-1 (Terms of Reference) defines the scope of the NADF, and SD-2 (Program Plan) describes issues of interest to it. The other documents describe the agreements needed for a cooperative service. The NADF relies on X.500(88) to the largest extent possible.

  • SD-3 covers the Directory service, such as quality of service, and SD-4 covers the Directory schema.
  • SD-8 describes agreements for the NADF Pilot.
  • SD-10 gives security and privacy policy, including a User Bill of Rights for entries and listings, and SD-11 covers the security mechanisms used in the Public Directory service.
sections.eli5: Each numbered paper covers one job, like what the service promises, what information it holds, and how to keep it safe.

sections.title: Naming and Sharing the Name Space
sections.content:
SD-5 explains how a national authority should structure its DIT subtree, then defines the naming scheme for the c=CA and c=US parts. The subtree is split into a public name-space, for objects with public recognition such as states, counties and businesses, and several private name-spaces, each managed by one public provider. SD-12 is the registry of these providers, and SD-6 gives guidelines for organizing a private name-space.

SD-7 covers how the DIT is mapped onto multiple Directory Management Domains. Because competing providers make a single manager of the public name-space impossible, each provider links the public name-space into its own private one. The shared information is limited to knowledge references and naming links. SD-9 describes the central authority, the CAN, that coordinates and distributes it.
sections.eli5: The public part of the phone book is shared by everyone, and each company keeps its own private pages. Signposts link the two.

sections.title: Availability and Status
sections.content: When written, the Standing Documents existed only in hardcopy and PostScript, not ASCII, so they could not be issued as informational RFCs. The memo lists three ways to get them: postal mail from the NADF Secretariat, anonymous FTP, and an e-mail archive server. It says security issues are not discussed in the memo.
sections.eli5: The papers were only on paper or in a special print format, so this memo told people where to ask for copies.
